title: Looking back: the sources
hookLine: Avot, Berakhot, the laws of return, the midrash
tomorrow: Noa owes one teacher a thank-you. which one, and why?

lines: ROTATE IT, AND IT'S A FACE.
TURN IT, AND TURN IT AGAIN.
cards: A photo that looks wrong on the screen until you rotate it, and then suddenly it's a face. Some things only make sense from the next angle. Noa's last Shabbat at home, the table crowded, Saba David at the end of it.
Someone asks what she's packing besides clothes, and Saba answers for her with a line from Pirkei Avot, the text the two of them have been reading by phone all summer.
A sage called Ben Bag Bag said of the Torah: turn it, and turn it again, for everything is in it.

teach.h: TURN IT, AND TURN IT AGAIN.
teach.b: That's how this path has read its sources: turning them.
Avot, the sayings of the sages, short enough to carry in a pocket. Berakhot, the tractate of blessings, which begins with a simple question: from what time may the evening Shema be said?
The laws of return, Maimonides' map of teshuvah, of turning back. And the midrash, the rabbis' stories that fill the gaps between the verses. None of them gets used up.
You turn them, and another face appears. Every year of this path you've opened them again, and each time they showed you something you'd walked right past.
Now turn this week once more. Moses on Nebo, shown the whole land: see it all.
A child's question about rules, answered with a story: the stories stay. Hillel's candles, one more each night: the practices stay. A scroll kissed by way of a fringe: the torah stays.
A grandfather's voice on a recording: the story stays. A sign above a sink, and Hillel on one foot: the ideas stay. Six turns, and the same Torah underneath.

how: Jewish study returns again and again to the same sources, Pirkei Avot, the Talmud's Berakhot, Maimonides' laws of teshuvah, the midrash, following Ben Bag Bag's saying: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it.

o: the books you read once and then put away
the path's sources, turned again and again
the footnotes that prove the lessons were true

games.q: the week of looking back — tap the pairs.
p: turn it, and turn it again

s: Ben Bag Bag says once you've learned the Torah, you've seen all of it
turn it and turn it again, for everything is in it.
Berakhot opens with a question about when to say the evening Shema
the tractate of blessings begins at nightfall.
the midrash replaces the verses with new stories
it fills the gaps between the verses; the verses stay.

games.q: a friend who finished a course on Pirkei Avot says she's done with it; she's read every line. what would Ben Bag Bag say?
o: turn it again; there's a face you haven't seen yet.
move on; a finished book has nothing left to give.
memorize it, so you never have to open it again.
games.why: Ben Bag Bag: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. the sources aren't used up by one reading.

practice: Count the week on your fingers, one line per finger: see it all, the stories stay, the practices stay, the torah stays, the story stays, the ideas stay. When you reach the last, hold that hand still.
Then bring back one saying from these years, any one, and say it quietly, turning it once in your mind.
